item.title: Teaching quantum mechanics in secondary schools: A qubit-first learning path to Bell's inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2610.29834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teaching quantum mechanics at the secondary school level remains a major educational challenge. Traditional historical approaches often present the theory as a sequence of disconnected phenomena, requiring extensive prior knowledge of classical physics before students can appreciate the conceptual structure of quantum physics. In this work, we present the design, implementation, and evaluation of a curriculum based on the two state (qubit first) approach, in which the fundamental postulates of quantum mechanics are introduced through mathematically accessible two level systems and realized with light polarization. The curriculum integrates theoretical instruction, laboratory activities, a coherent progression grounded in the interactive simulations, and inquiry based learning into a coherent pathway that progresses from quantum states and superposition to entanglement and the experimental violation of Bell's inequalities. A distinctive feature of the project is the experimental realization of the violation of Bell's inequalities obtained in a newly established quantum optics laboratory in an Italian high school, where students performed, for the first time in Italy, an authentic Bell test using polarization-entangled photons. The same educational framework was adopted for in service teacher professional development courses. Learning outcomes were evaluated through mixed methods. Preliminary analysis indicates significant improvements in conceptual understanding, confidence in using mathematical formalism, and appreciation of the relationship between theory, experimentation, and the foundations of quantum mechanics. The proposed curriculum shows that two-state formalism and supported by real laboratory experiences enables secondary-school students to engage more meaningfully with both the conceptual foundations of quantum mechanics and their experimental verification.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Carlini, Andrea Lanza, Dalida Monti, Anna Soso, Elena Losero, Maddalena Mari, Matteo O\~nate Orozco, Maria Bondani

item.title: Light pulse propagation through a dielectric slab. I. Retarded integral equations and their local finite-difference solution
item.description: arXiv:2610.29336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We describe the propagation of a nonresonant light pulse normally incident on a thin dielectric slab using an integral-equation approach to electromagnetism. This emerges naturally from the microscopic picture of the material as made of polarizable atoms, confined within the material vacuum volume by their bonding interactions, each responding to the input radiation pulse as well as to the re-radiated pulses of the other atoms to which it is causally connected. The retarded integral equations are shown to be exactly equivalent to a local wave equation coupled to an auxiliary Lorentz-oscillator equation, which we solve numerically with a finite-difference time-domain scheme. For a slab thick enough that the front- and back-surface reflections are temporally separated, the front-surface reflectivity extracted from the simulation agrees with the Fresnel formula to within 1 percent, and the back-surface echo appears at exactly the expected round-trip delay. For a slab thinner than one optical cycle, the multiply-reflected wavelets overlap and interfere, and a full space-time map of the field directly visualizes the build-up of thin-film-like interference in the time domain. The material parameters used here are illustrative rather than fitted to measured data, and the numerical scheme is verified by an explicit grid-convergence study. In a companion paper (Paper II) the retarded integral equations are solved directly, without the local reformulation, and the two independent numerical solutions are shown to agree.
item.dc:creator: Giancarlo Reali (University of Pavia)

item.title: Data-driven modeling in the introductory physics laboratory: Scaling analysis and data collapse in the specific heat of water experiment
item.description: arXiv:2609.15124v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a data-driven redesign of the classic specific-heat-of-water experiment that uses scaling analysis and data collapse for model construction rather than beginning with a previously established thermodynamic formula. The activity combines structured experimental and analytical guidance with instructor-mediated questioning, while the thermodynamic description is deliberately postponed. Students collect temperature-time data under different conditions and obtain a collapsed relation between the mass-normalized energy input and temperature rise through successive rescaling. They formulate an empirical model from this relation and test it using additional data not included in its construction. In the post-experimental discussion, the thermodynamic description shows that the fitted empirical constant characterizes the combined response of the water and calorimeter and approximates a quantity that depends weakly on water mass. Reanalysis of the mass-dependent data separates the two contributions, with limited precision over the available water-mass range. The copper cup is an intentional feature of the instructional design: its contribution is large enough to require physical interpretation but varies little enough over the explored mass range for the data to collapse approximately onto a single relation. The same apparatus thereby supports empirical model construction, thermodynamic interpretation, and separation of the component contributions.
item.dc:creator: Kazumasa Kushida, Tomohiro Oda, Koji Yamaguchi
